rows.stem: Which of the following, compounds is most reactive towards nucleophilic substitution reaction with aqueous NaOH ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — all four options are DRAWN Kekule benzene rings and the stem names nothing. Read off the page at 8x zoom and rendered as condensed formulae plus their names (a lossless reading, not an approximation; naming states no more than the drawing does). The ring orientation is identical in all four, with vertices at top, upper-left, lower-left, bottom, lower-right and upper-right: (A) Cl at the upper-right vertex only; (B) Cl at the upper-right, CH3 at the lower-right (ortho) and H3C at the lower-left, i.e. 2,4; (C) Cl at the upper-right and CH3O at the lower-left, i.e. PARA; (D) Cl at the upper-right, NO2 at the lower-right and O2N at the lower-left, i.e. 2,4. Page idx 4.
rows.solution:
A halogen attached directly to a benzene ring is normally very unreactive towards nucleophiles, because its lone pair is delocalised into the ring and the \(\mathrm{C-Cl}\) bond gains partial double bond character. What changes that is an electron-WITHDRAWING group placed ortho or para to the halogen.

When hydroxide attacks such a ring, the intermediate carries a negative charge, and a nitro group at the ortho or para position can take that charge onto its own oxygen atoms by resonance. Two nitro groups, at positions 2 and 4, stabilise it twice over, so 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene reacts readily with aqueous sodium hydroxide. The methyl and methoxy groups do the opposite — both release electron density into the ring — so those two compounds are even less reactive than chlorobenzene itself.

rows.stem: The dehydration of 1°, 2° and 3° alcohols follows the order :
rows.solution:
Acid catalysed dehydration proceeds through a carbocation, formed when the protonated alcohol loses water in the slow step. The reaction is therefore as fast as that carbocation is stable, and alkyl groups stabilise a carbocation by releasing electron density towards the positive centre.

A tertiary alcohol gives a tertiary carbocation with three alkyl groups, a secondary alcohol gives one with two, and a primary alcohol would give one with a single group — so unstable that primary alcohols in fact dehydrate by a concerted route and need much harsher conditions. The order of ease of dehydration is \(3^{\circ} > 2^{\circ} > 1^{\circ}\).

rows.subtopic: Definitions of Some Important Terms Pertaining to Coordination Compounds
rows.stem: The oxidation number of Co in \(\mathrm{[Co(NH_3)_5\,(ONO)]\,SO_4}\) is :
rows.solution:
The sulphate ion outside the coordination sphere carries \(-2\), so the complex cation must be \(+2\). Inside it, the five ammine ligands are neutral and the nitrito ligand — written ONO because it is attached through oxygen — carries \(-1\). For the cation to be \(+2\), cobalt must therefore be \(+3\).

Note that the ambidentate nitrito ligand carries the same \(-1\) charge whichever atom it binds through, so the \(\mathrm{ONO}\) notation affects the NAME of the complex but not the oxidation state.

rows.stem: Which reagent is used to distinguish between \(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2}\) and \(\mathrm{(C_2H_5)_2NH}\) ?
rows.solution:
The two amines differ in one thing: the primary amine has two hydrogens on nitrogen and the secondary has one. The carbylamine test responds to that difference. Warmed with chloroform and ethanolic potassium hydroxide, a PRIMARY amine gives an isocyanide with an unmistakably foul smell:
\(\mathrm{C_2H_5NH_2} + \mathrm{CHCl_3} + 3\mathrm{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_2H_5NC} + 3\mathrm{KCl} + 3\mathrm{H_2O}\)
Diethylamine, being secondary, gives no reaction at all.

Potassium permanganate is a general oxidant and distinguishes nothing here; sodium hydroxide with iodine is the iodoform test, for methyl ketones and certain alcohols; and neutral ferric chloride is the test for phenols.

rows.stem: Among the following, which one has the lowest value of \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) ?
rows.figureNote: REQUIRED — all four options are DRAWN structures and the stem names nothing. Read off the page at 3.2x zoom and rendered as condensed formulae plus their names (a lossless reading): every ring carries an inner circle, i.e. benzene; (B) and (C) are PARA-disubstituted, with the two substituents on opposite horizontal vertices, while (A) and (D) are monosubstituted. Page idx 6.
rows.solution:
A lower \(\mathrm{pK_b}\) means a stronger base, so the question is which nitrogen holds its lone pair most available.

In aniline, 4-methylaniline and 4-nitroaniline the nitrogen is attached directly to the ring, so its lone pair is delocalised into the \(\pi\) system and much less available to a proton. In benzylamine a \(\mathrm{CH_2}\) group stands between the nitrogen and the ring, which breaks that conjugation completely: the lone pair stays on nitrogen and the compound behaves like an ordinary aliphatic amine.

Among the three anilines the methyl group helps a little and the nitro group hurts a great deal, but none of them can match benzylamine, which is the strongest base here and therefore has the lowest \(\mathrm{pK_b}\).

rows.subtopic: Some Important Compounds of Transition Elements
rows.stem: In aqueous acidified solution, \(\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}}\) ion converts to which of the following ?
rows.solution:
Chromate and dichromate are interconvertible and the pH decides which one is present. In acidic solution the yellow chromate is converted to the orange dichromate:
\(2\mathrm{CrO_4^{2-}} + 2\mathrm{H^+} \longrightarrow \mathrm{Cr_2O_7^{2-}} + \mathrm{H_2O}\)
Adding alkali reverses it. Chromium remains at \(+6\) throughout, so this is not a redox change: reaching \(\mathrm{Cr^{3+}}\) would need a reducing agent as well as acid, and neither \(\mathrm{CrO}\) nor \(\mathrm{CrO_3}\) is formed in aqueous acid.

rows.stem: The boiling point of an azeotropic mixture of water and nitric acid is more than that of pure water and nitric acid. The mixture shows :

options.label: B
options.text: that solution is an ideal solution

rows.solution: A maximum boiling azeotrope is the signature of negative deviation. In a mixture of water and nitric acid the two kinds of molecule attract each other more strongly than each attracts its own kind, so after mixing the molecules are held in the liquid more tightly than before. Fewer escape, each partial vapour pressure falls below the value Raoult's law predicts, and the total vapour pressure is lowered. A mixture with a lowered vapour pressure must be heated further before it can match the external pressure, which is exactly why this azeotrope boils above either pure component.

rows.stem: On hydrolysis, which of the following carbohydrates gives only glucose ?
rows.solution: Galactose is a monosaccharide, so it does not hydrolyse at all. Sucrose hydrolyses to one glucose and one fructose, and lactose to one glucose and one galactose, so both give a second sugar alongside glucose. Starch is a polysaccharide built entirely of \(\alpha\)-D-glucose units — amylose with \(\mathrm{C_1-C_4}\) linkages and amylopectin with \(\mathrm{C_1-C_6}\) branches as well — so complete hydrolysis gives glucose and nothing else.

rows.stem: For the reaction \(\mathrm{2A \rightarrow 3B}\), the rate of reaction \(+\dfrac{\mathrm{d\,[B]}}{\mathrm{dt}}\) is equal to :
rows.solution:
Rates of appearance and disappearance are tied together by the stoichiometric coefficients. For \(2\mathrm{A} \longrightarrow 3\mathrm{B}\) the single rate of reaction is
\(-\dfrac{1}{2}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt} = +\dfrac{1}{3}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{B}]}{dt}\)

Multiplying through by 3,
\(\dfrac{d[\mathrm{B}]}{dt} = -\dfrac{3}{2}\dfrac{d[\mathrm{A}]}{dt}\)

The minus sign is required: \(d[\mathrm{A}]/dt\) is itself negative because A is being consumed, so the minus makes the right-hand side positive, as it must be for a species being formed.

rows.subtopic: General Properties of the Transition Elements (d-Block)
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Separation of Zr and Hf is difficult.
Reason (R) : Zr and Hf have almost identical atomic and ionic radii due to lanthanoid contraction.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution: Zirconium and hafnium are genuinely hard to separate, so the Assertion is true, and the Reason names the cause exactly. Hafnium follows the lanthanoids, whose 4f electrons shield the nuclear charge poorly, so the outer shells are drawn in across that series; by the time hafnium is reached it has almost the same atomic and ionic radii as zirconium, one period above it. Nearly identical size means nearly identical chemistry, and separation is correspondingly difficult. The Reason is therefore the correct explanation of the Assertion.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Phenol is more acidic than 4-methylphenol.
Reason (R) : The presence of an electron releasing group in phenol makes it more acidic.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Phenol IS more acidic than 4-methylphenol, so the Assertion is true. Acidity is decided by how stable the phenoxide ion is once the proton has gone, and the methyl group of 4-methylphenol releases electron density towards that negative charge, destabilising it and making the compound the weaker acid.

The Reason inverts that logic. An electron-releasing group makes a phenol LESS acidic, not more. So the Assertion is true while the Reason is false.

rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Aromatic primary amines can easily be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis.
Reason (R) : Gabriel phthalimide synthesis is used to prepare only aliphatic primary amines.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Aromatic primary amines cannot be prepared by Gabriel phthalimide synthesis, so the Assertion is false. The Reason states correctly that the method serves only aliphatic primary amines, so it is true.

The underlying reason, which neither statement gives, is that the synthesis relies on the phthalimide anion displacing a halide by nucleophilic substitution, and an aryl halide will not undergo that substitution — its \(\mathrm{C-X}\) bond has partial double bond character and the electron-rich ring repels the nucleophile. So the Assertion is false while the Reason is true.

rows.subtopic: Factors Influencing Rate of a Reaction
rows.stem:
Assertion (A) : Order of reaction is not applicable for elementary reaction but applicable for complex reaction.
Reason (R) : Order of reaction is an experimental quantity.
rows.context: For Questions number 13 to 16, two statements are given — one labelled as Assertion (A) and the other labelled as Reason (R). Select the correct answer to these questions from the codes (A), (B), (C) and (D) as given below :

options.label: A
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true and Reason (R) is the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: B
options.text: Both Assertion (A) and Reason (R) are true, but Reason (R) is not the correct explanation of the Assertion (A).

options.label: C
options.text: Assertion (A) is true, but Reason (R) is false.

options.label: D
options.text: Assertion (A) is false, but Reason (R) is true.

rows.solution:
Order applies to elementary and complex reactions alike, so the Assertion, which says it does not apply to elementary reactions, is false. It is MOLECULARITY that is restricted, being defined only for a single elementary step and therefore meaningless for a multi-step reaction.

The Reason is true: order is determined from the experimentally measured rate law rather than read off the balanced equation. So the Assertion is false while the Reason is true.

rows.stem:
How do you explain the following ?
(a) Presence of a carbonyl group in glucose
(b) Presence of five – OH groups in glucose
rows.solution:
(a) The carbonyl group. Glucose reacts with hydroxylamine to give an oxime, and with hydrogen cyanide to give a cyanohydrin:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} + \mathrm{H_2N-OH} \longrightarrow \mathrm{CH{=}N-OH(CHOH)_4CH_2OH}\)
Both are addition reactions characteristic of a carbonyl group, so a carbonyl group must be present. That it is an aldehyde rather than a ketone follows separately, from glucose reducing Tollens' reagent and being oxidised by bromine water.

(b) The five hydroxyl groups. Glucose reacts with acetic anhydride to give a stable pentaacetate, a derivative carrying exactly five acetyl groups. Acetylation occurs at hydroxyl groups, so there must be five of them:
\(\mathrm{CHO(CHOH)_4CH_2OH} \xrightarrow{(\mathrm{CH_3CO})_2\mathrm{O}} \mathrm{CHO(CH{-}OCOCH_3)_4CH_2{-}OCOCH_3}\)
That they sit on five different carbons follows from the derivative being stable: two hydroxyl groups on one carbon would make a gem-diol, which loses water at once.

rows.stem:
Give reasons for the following :
(a) Alkyl halides, though polar, yet their solubility in water is very low.
(b) p-Dichlorobenzene has higher melting point than those of o- and m-isomers.
(c) \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) – I is more reactive than \(\mathrm{CH_3}\) – Br towards \(\mathrm{S_N2}\) reactions.
rows.solution:
(a) Dissolving anything in water means breaking the hydrogen bonds that water molecules make with one another, and that costs energy which must be repaid by the new attractions formed. An alkyl halide is polar, so it does set up dipole-dipole attractions with water — but it has no hydrogen bonded to a strongly electronegative atom, so it cannot form hydrogen bonds with water itself. The energy released by the new, weaker attractions does not repay the cost of breaking the old, stronger ones, so alkyl halides dissolve only very slightly.

(b) The para isomer is the most symmetrical of the three, so its molecules pack into the crystal lattice more closely and more regularly. A better packed lattice takes more energy to break down, so p-dichlorobenzene melts at the higher temperature. Note that this argument concerns the SOLID state only: boiling points follow dipole moment instead, and there the para isomer, being non-polar, comes out lowest.

(c) In an \(\mathrm{S_N}2\) reaction the rate depends on how readily the leaving group departs, and iodide is the better leaving group of the two. Iodine is the larger atom, so the \(\mathrm{C-I}\) bond is longer and weaker than the \(\mathrm{C-Br}\) bond and breaks more easily; the larger iodide ion also spreads its negative charge over a bigger volume and is the more stable of the two anions. Methyl iodide is therefore the more reactive.

rows.stem:
How will you obtain the following from benzene diazonium chloride ? Write chemical equations involved :
(a) Phenol
(b) Iodobenzene
(c) p-Aminoazobenzene
rows.solution:
All three start by replacing or attacking the diazonium group, which is what makes diazonium salts so useful in synthesis.

(a) Phenol. Warming the aqueous solution of the diazonium salt is enough: water acts as the nucleophile, nitrogen is expelled as gas, and the hydroxyl group takes its place.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{H_2O} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \mathrm{C_6H_5OH} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{HCl}\)

(b) Iodobenzene. Iodide is exceptional among the halides here: it needs no copper catalyst, and simply warming the diazonium salt with potassium iodide gives the aryl iodide.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{KI} \longrightarrow \mathrm{C_6H_5I} + \mathrm{N_2} + \mathrm{KCl}\)

(c) p-Aminoazobenzene. This one is a COUPLING, not a replacement: the diazonium group is kept. In mildly acidic solution the diazonium ion acts as a weak electrophile and attacks aniline at the position para to its amino group.
\(\mathrm{C_6H_5N_2^+Cl^-} + \mathrm{C_6H_5NH_2} \xrightarrow{\mathrm{H^+}} \mathrm{C_6H_5-N{=}N-C_6H_4-NH_2\ (p)} + \mathrm{HCl}\)
The product is a yellow dye. Coupling works only with strongly activated rings — phenols and amines — which is why the other two parts had to replace the group instead.
